frase_gancho.texto: Two serpents form her face, and others weave her skirt.

puente_narrativo.texto: After the image of the Sun and the ages of the world, we come to the image of the earth, another great force in Mexica thought.

guion_corto.texto: Coatlicue means “the one with the skirt of serpents,” and the name is literal. Where the head should be, there are two serpents in profile, facing each other, and between their fangs a face takes shape. From her chest hangs a necklace of hands and hearts with a skull at the center, and her feet end in eagle talons. This is a Mexica work from the Late Postclassic, and it represents the goddess of the earth, mother of Huitzilopochtli. It was discovered on August 13, 1790, in the Main Square of Mexico City. Its appearance disturbed the viceregal authorities so much that they buried it again. For the Mexica, the earth gave life and also received the dead. That is why this mother does not smile. She holds both things at once.

guion_largo.texto:
Coatlicue is one of the best-known sculptures of Mexica art, and also one of the most unsettling. It is a work from the Late Postclassic. It appeared on August 13, 1790, in the Main Square of Mexico City, in the heart of what was once Tenochtitlan.

Her name means “the one with the skirt of serpents,” and the sculptor took it literally. The skirt is a weave of interlaced rattlesnakes. Where the head should be, there are two serpents in profile, facing each other, and their jaws form a face that is not human. From the chest hangs a necklace of severed hands and hearts, with a skull at the center. The legs end in eagle talons with feathers.

If you could turn her over, you would find another surprise. On the underside of the base, Tlaltecuhtli, the deity of the earth, is carved. That image faced the ground, out of sight.

For the Mexica, Coatlicue was the mother of the gods. According to the myth of Coatepec, she was the mother of Huitzilopochtli, of Coyolxauhqui, and of the stars. When her children rose up against her, Huitzilopochtli was born fully armed and defended her. That the earth should have such a terrible appearance was not a contradiction. It is thought that, for the Mexica, the same earth gave life and also received the dead.

After its discovery, the sculpture disturbed the viceregal authorities so much that they decided to bury it again, in the courtyard of the Royal University. They feared it would awaken devotion among the Indigenous people. It remained hidden until 1825, when it was finally taken out for the National Museum. More than two centuries after its discovery, it still unsettles those who look at it.

texto: Look for the two serpents in profile facing each other where the head should be.
Find the necklace of hands and hearts with a skull at the center.
Recognize the skirt woven from serpents and the feet with eagle talons.

texto.Dimensions: 252 cm high x 158 cm wide x 124 cm thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: Coatlicue is a monster invented only to frighten people.
texto.respuesta: Reality: She is the Mexica goddess of the earth and motherhood, mother of Huitzilopochtli. Her terrible features are part of that symbolism and are not mere macabre decoration.
